glosses: To give a sermon.

examples.text: The minister has just preached from the Book of Psalms.

glosses: To proclaim by public discourse; to utter in a sermon or a formal religious harangue.

examples.text: The Spirit of the Lord God is vpon me, therefore hathe the Lord anointed me: he hathe ſent me to preache good tidings vnto the poore,[…]

glosses: To advise or recommend earnestly.

examples.text: My Mʳ preaches patience to him,[…]

glosses: To teach or instruct by preaching; to inform by preaching.

examples.text: The Spirits of the Dead, / Quitting their mortal mansion, enter not, / As falsely ye are preached, their final seat / Of bliss, or bale;[…]

glosses: To give advice in an offensive or obtrusive manner.
A religious discourse.

examples.text: he make peace in his preaches and play with esteem

glosses: Used to express strong agreement (as if encouraging somebody to continue speaking).

examples.text: – If you can't do the time, don't do the crime! – Preach!

glosses: A spoken lesson or exposition, usually delivered to a group.

examples.text: During class today the professor delivered an interesting lecture.

The stories did not seem to me to touch life. […] They left me with the impression of a well-delivered stereopticon lecture, with characters about as life-like as the shadows on the screen, and whisking on and off, at the mercy of the operator.

glosses: A class that primarily consists of a (weekly or other regularly held) lecture (as in sense 1), usually at college or university.

examples.text: We will not have lecture tomorrow.
Lecture notes are online.

glosses: A berating or scolding, especially if lengthy, formal or given in a stern or angry manner.

examples.text: I really don't want you to give me a lecture about my bad eating habits.

glosses: The act of reading.

examples.text: the lecture of Holy Scripture

glosses: To teach (somebody) by giving a speech on a given topic.

examples.text: The professor lectured to two classes this morning.

glosses: To preach, to berate, to scold.

examples.text: Emily's father lectured her about the importance of being home before midnight.

glosses: To make moral reflections (on, upon, about or over something); to regard acts and events as involving a moral.

examples.text:
1589, Robert Greene, Menaphon, London: Sampson Clarke, “Arcadia,”
[…] his Ladie reaching him a Marigold, he began to moralize of it thus merely. I meruaile the Poets that were so prodigall in painting the amorous affection of the Sunne to his Hyacinth, did neuer obserue the relation of loue twixt him and the Marigold:

1741, Samuel Richardson, Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded, London: S. Richardson and J. Osborn,, Volume 3, Letter 8, p. 38,
[…] I shall not make an unworthy Correspondent altogether; for I can get into thy grave Way, and moralize a little now-and-then:

One hoped, and the other despaired: they chose their own lots, and were righteously doomed to endure them. But you’ll not want to hear my moralising, Mr. Lockwood; you’ll judge, as well as I can, all these things:
The usual conduct of the spoilt child! Had she not witnessed it, and moralized upon it, in other families?

I depended on Philip now, for I had nothing, not even seven cents for carfare. I could be certain, however, that he wouldn’t moralize at me, he’d set about dressing me, he’d scrounge a sweater among his neighborhood acquaintances […]

glosses: To say (something) expressing a moral reflection or judgment.

examples.text: “Unless I heard the whole repeated, I cannot continue it,” she said. / “Yet it was quickly learned, ‘soon gained, soon gone,’” moralized the tutor.

1929, Virginia Woolf, “Geraldine and Jane” in The Common Reader, Second Series, London: The Hogarth Press, 1935, p. 191,
“The more one loves, the more helpless one feels”, she moralised.

glosses: To render moral; to correct the morals of; to give the appearance of morality to.

examples.text:
Let gratefull Aromatick odours burne,
Let pious incense smoake, for the returne

More Art, then raised Athens to her pride,
More civill Ethicks he containe, then may
Well moralize all sauage India.

What, then, does he want? As always, what he appears to want is a moralised version of the existing thing—the old type of school, but with no caning, no bullying or underfeeding, and not quite so much Greek.

glosses: To give a moral quality to; to affect the moral quality of, either for better or worse.

examples.text:

examples.text: Did he not moralize this spectacle?

glosses: To supply with moral lessons, teachings, or examples; to lend a moral to.

examples.text:

In every babbling brook he finds a friend,
